readers.reasoning: Per OpenACC 3.4 a derived-type variable in a data clause copies its members, but data behind allocatable members is not copied. copy(x%a) separately allocates and copies the allocatable component, so listing both is the intended way to transfer such data. No rule forbids a member and its parent in the same construct. The gfortran message is an implementation restriction. Some uncertainty about attachment semantics.

OpenACC 3.4 data-clause restrictions do not forbid naming a derived-type variable in copyin and one of its allocatable members in copy on the same directive. Copying x does not copy data reached through an allocatable member, so x%a is separate data. The gfortran message is its own diagnostic. The spec text on overlapping or aliased data is thin, so required acceptance is not certain.

copyin(x) copies the derived type but not the data behind the allocatable member; copy(x%a) then copies that member and attaches it. A member of a derived type may appear in a data clause, and the restrictions only prohibit array notation on a parent. The parallel loop is independent, giving r1=4160. Rejecting the mix of x and x%a is a compiler error.

Fortran derived type x with an allocatable member. copyin(x) copies the members but not the data behind the allocatable member; copy(x%a) is a separate member var that allocates and attaches that data. OpenACC 3.4 allows composite members in data clauses and has no rule against a variable and its member in the same construct. The gfortran-style error about mixed component and non-component access is not a spec rule, so refusing the program is not permitted.

adjudicators.reasoning: Reading A's conclusion holds. Copying x does not copy data reached through the allocatable member, so x%a is separate data. The restrictions in 3.4 forbid subarray notation on a member together with subarray notation on a parent; here no subarray notation is used. No rule forbids a member and its parent in data clauses of one construct. The compiler's mixed-access error is its own limitation. Reading B's doubt is unsupported by any restricting text.

A member of a composite variable is a valid var, and no OpenACC 3.4 restriction forbids a derived-type variable and one of its members in data clauses of the same directive. The array-notation restriction on parents of members is for update and does not apply (no subarray notation here). Copying x does not copy data behind allocatable member a, so copy(x%a) transfers it. The gfortran message is an implementation limit. Reading A is right; Reading B's doubt rests on thin text, not on a rule against it.
